title: NLL-Guided Full-Attention Layer Selection for Training-Free Sliding-Window Adaptation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to decide which layers of a pretrained Transformer should retain full attention when adapting to hybrid sliding-window attention without training. This objective is not explicitly covered by any prior paper. While papers like [1], [20], and [22] discuss hybrid attention architectures and their challenges, none focus on layer selection for retaining full attention during adaptation. Papers such as [7], [9], and [14] discuss layer-wise pruning or dropping, but their purpose is computational efficiency or compression, not optimizing layer retention for hybrid attention adaptation.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves NLL-guided layer selection: measuring each layer's negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention, and keeping the most sensitive layers at full attention. Papers like [8], [10], [21], and [33] discuss layer sensitivity analysis for quantization or pruning, but none use negative log-likelihood degradation as the sensitivity metric for hybrid attention adaptation. Papers such as [20] and [22] discuss sliding-window attention but do not propose a mechanism for layer selection based on NLL degradation.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, achieving 64.6% accuracy with only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) at half the budget. Papers like [1], [20], and [22] evaluate hybrid attention architectures, but none use LongMemEval or a similar benchmark family. The evaluation design (comparing accuracy and computational budget trade-offs for hybrid attention configurations) is not explicitly covered by any prior paper.

### Domain
The domain is efficient long-context LLM inference. This domain is covered by multiple prior papers, including [1], [3], [5], [6], [11], [19], [20], and [22], which all address efficient long-context processing for LLMs. While the specific problem of layer selection for hybrid sliding-window attention is new, the general application area of efficient long-context LLM inference is well-established.

## PURPOSE

The purpose is: "Decide which layers of a pretrained Transformer should retain full attention when adapting to hybrid sliding-window attention without training."

Paper [20] (SWAA) directly addresses "Sliding Window Attention Adaptation for Efficient and Quality Preserving Long Context Processing" — adapting pretrained full-attention models to use sliding-window attention. Paper [1] addresses "post-training linearisation methods convert pre-trained Transformers to linear models efficiently, often using hybrid approaches that combine linear attention with sliding-window softmax" and identifies flaws in existing hybrid methods. Paper [11] also covers "converting pre-trained softmax attention blocks" to hybrid architectures. Paper [22] studies hybrid architectures combining sliding-window and global attention layers.

However, the specific purpose of *selecting which layers* to keep as full attention (layer selection for hybrid conversion without training) is most directly addressed by [20], which explicitly deals with which layers use SWA vs. full attention in a pretrained model adaptation setting. Paper [1] also addresses component imbalance in hybrid linear attention conversion, touching on layer-level decisions.

## MECHANISM

The mechanism is: "NLL-guided layer selection — measure each layer's NLL degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention, and keep the most sensitive layers at full attention."

This is a sensitivity-based layer selection approach using loss/NLL as the sensitivity metric. Papers [8], [21], [29], [33], [31], [34] all use layer-wise sensitivity analysis (measuring per-layer degradation) to guide mixed-precision decisions — the same primitive of "measure how much performance degrades when layer X is changed, use that to decide treatment of layer X." Paper [21] (LSMQ) explicitly "calculated the sensitivity of each layer first, then the weight of each layer would be automatically quantized." Paper [29] assigns "higher bit precisions to layers that are more sensitive." Paper [33] proposes "an accuracy-aware criterion to quantify the layer's importance rank."

The primitive is identical: isolate each layer's contribution to output quality degradation, rank layers by sensitivity, allocate a higher-quality operation to the most sensitive layers. The application domain differs (quantization vs. attention type selection) but the mechanism is the same.

## EVALUATION

The evaluation uses LongMemEval benchmark with accuracy metric, comparing against a periodic baseline (1/2-FA) at different budget levels. Paper [20] evaluates sliding-window attention adaptation on long-context benchmarks. Paper [3] evaluates long-context inference efficiency on LLM benchmarks with accuracy metrics. The evaluation design (accuracy on a long-context QA benchmark, comparing sparse-attention variants at different budgets) is used in [20] and [3]. LongMemEval is a specific benchmark instance within the long-context evaluation design family used across these papers.

## DOMAIN

The domain is "Efficient long-context LLM inference." Papers [3], [5], [6], [19], [20] all operate in this exact domain. Paper [20] is directly in efficient long-context LLM inference with sliding-window attention. Paper [3] addresses "Efficient Long-Context Inference... for LLMs."
